#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Census of Agriculture
Description: The Census of Agriculture, conducted once every five years, looks at land use and ownership, producer characteristics, production practices, income, and expenditures. The Census of Agriculture is a complete count of U.S. farms and ranches and the people who operate them. Even small plots of land - whether rural or urban - count if $1,000 or more of agricultural products were produced and sold, or normally would have been sold, during the census year.
URL: https://nass.usda.gov/AgCensus

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Census of Agriculture
Description: The Census of Agriculture, conducted once every five years, looks at land use and ownership, producer characteristics, production practices, income, and expenditures. The Census of Agriculture is a complete count of U.S. farms and ranches and the people who operate them. Even small plots of land - whether rural or urban - count if $1,000 or more of agricultural products were produced and sold, or normally would have been sold, during the census year.
URL: https://nass.usda.gov/AgCensus

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Census of Agriculture: Research Report

## Summary

The Census of Agriculture is the only source of consistent, comparable agricultural data for every U.S. county, state and territory. It is published by USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) under the Census of Agriculture Act of 1997. Federal statisticians have collected it in some form since 1840, and in the current agricultural census series since 1850. The most recent edition covers 2022 and was released on February 13, 2024. The next covers 2027: OMB approved the questionnaire in September 2026, and the census will be mailed in late 2027 or early 2028. It is a high-value dataset, and it is preserved fairly well. The main risks today are low response rates, deep staff cuts at NASS, and a USDA push to rely more on administrative and satellite data.

## 1. Checking your description

Your description is accurate. It closely matches NASS's own wording. A few details are worth adding:

- **URL:** https://nass.usda.gov/AgCensus works. It resolves to `https://www.nass.usda.gov/AgCensus/`, page title "USDA – National Agricultural Statistics Service – Census of Agriculture."
- **Wording:** NASS's page metadata still says "operator characteristics," while newer materials say "producer characteristics." Since 2017 the census has collected data on up to four "producers" per farm instead of one "principal operator," which is a known break in comparability.
- **The $1,000 threshold isn't universal:**
  - It applies in the 50 states, Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands.
  - Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands use $500.
  - American Samoa has no threshold and also counts food grown for home use.
- **The threshold has never been inflation-adjusted.** It was first used in 1974. The farm definition has changed nine times since 1850, when the bar was $100 in sales.
- **"Complete count" is the legal goal, not a literal description of the numbers.** Published figures are adjusted for undercoverage, nonresponse and misclassification (see section 7). They are estimates, not raw tallies.

## 2. Who publishes it

- **Publisher:** National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS), U.S. Department of Agriculture. Address: 1400 Independence Ave. SW, Washington, DC 20250.
- **Data help line:** (800) 727-9540. Media: NASS-Media@usda.gov.
- **Agency background:** NASS traces its roots to USDA's Division of Statistics (1863). The Crop Reporting Board, now the Agricultural Statistics Board, was created in 1905. A 1961 reorganization created the Statistical Reporting Service, which later became NASS.
- **Before 1997:** For 156 years (1840–1996), the Commerce Department's Census Bureau ran the agricultural census.

## 3. Legal authority

- **Mandate:** Census of Agriculture Act of 1997 (Pub. L. 105-113, codified at 7 U.S.C. 2204g). It requires the Secretary of Agriculture to conduct the census every five years. It was signed November 21, 1997, partway through the 1997 cycle.
- **Response is mandatory.** The 2027 form states: "Response to this survey is required by law under Title 7 USC 2204(g) Public Law 105-113." This also covers the screening form and related special studies.
- **Confidentiality protections:**
  - 7 U.S.C. 2276
  - 18 U.S.C. 1905
  - CIPSEA 2018 (Title III of Pub. L. 115-435)
  - Data may be used only for statistical purposes, and only totals are published. Anyone who willfully discloses identifiable information faces fines and/or jail.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act:**
  - OMB control number 0535-0226.
  - The 2027 collection was approved "with change" on September 16, 2026, and the approval expires September 30, 2029.
  - Estimated burden: about 14.1 million responses and 2.86 million hours.
  - Estimated annual federal cost: $53.4 million.
  - Average completion time: 50 minutes.
- **Timing law:** Pub. L. 94-229 (1976) shortened the gap after the 1974 census so the census now covers years ending in 2 and 7, in step with the Economic Census.

## 4. History

| Period | Milestone |
|---|---|
| 1810/1820 | The decennial population census first asked about agriculture. |
| 1840 | First separate agriculture schedules, part of the Sixth Decennial Census. |
| 1850–1920 | Part of the decennial census. 1850 gave the first formal farm definition ($100 in sales). |
| 1915 / 1925 | Congress authorized a five-year census. Mid-decade censuses followed in 1925, 1935 and 1945. |
| 1950s–1974 | Reference years ending in 4 and 9. |
| 1974 | The current $1,000 farm definition begins. |
| 1978 → 1982 | Shift to years ending in 2 and 7. |
| 1997 | Responsibility moves to NASS. 1997 is the first NASS-run census. |
| 2012 | NASS and Cornell's Mann Library put the digitized 1840–2007 reports online. |
| 2017 | New producer demographics, with up to four producers per farm. |
| 2022 | Released February 13, 2024. Response rate 61%, with more than 40% responding online. |
| 2027 | Mail list is being built through the National Agricultural Classification Survey (NACS): about 250,000 forms in 2024, plus a 2026 version. NASS took content requests in 2024 (89 FR 58715). Notices ran January and May 2026, and OMB approved in September 2026. |

Notable fact: U.S. farm numbers peaked in 1935 at 6,812,350, with an average size of 154.8 acres.

## 5. What it contains and how it's published

**Subjects covered:** number and size of farms, land use and tenure, crops and livestock, market value of sales, production expenses, net cash farm income, government payments, land and building values, machinery, practices (conservation, organic, precision agriculture, internet access), and producer demographics (age, sex, race and ethnicity, veteran status, new and beginning producers).

**2022 headline numbers:**
- 1,900,487 farms, down 6.9% from 2017.
- 880.1 million acres, or 39% of U.S. land.
- Average farm size 463 acres.
- $543 billion in agricultural products sold, against $424 billion in production expenses.
- Net cash farm income of $152 billion. Only 43% of farms had positive net cash income.
- Family farms were 95% of farms and operated 84% of farmland.

**Geographic levels:** nation, state, county, congressional district, watershed, American Indian reservation and ZIP code. Outlying areas are published separately: Puerto Rico (July 2024), and the Northern Mariana Islands, U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa and Guam (February–April 2025).

**Main publications:**
- **Volume 1:** national, state and county tables.
- **Volume 2:** Subject Series.
- Highlights, State and County Profiles, Congressional District Profiles (May 2024), Race/Ethnicity/Gender Profiles.

**Follow-on studies funded under the census program:**
- Census of Aquaculture (2023 edition, released December 2024)
- Census of Horticultural Specialties (2024)
- Irrigation and Water Management Survey (2023 edition, released October 2024)
- Tenure, Ownership and Transition of Agricultural Land (TOTAL)
- Organic Survey
- Local Food Marketing Practices study
- Annual Current Agricultural Industrial Reports

**Ways to get the data:**
- **Quick Stats** (quickstats.nass.usda.gov): searchable database. It holds census data from 1997 on, plus survey data.
- **Quick Stats API:** requires a free key.
- **Bulk downloads** at nass.usda.gov/datasets (large compressed text files).
- PDFs and tables of every report.
- **Restricted microdata and special tabulations,** by request ("Special Tabulations and Restricted Microdata" page).
- **Census Data Query Tool:** its link now appears commented out of NASS's site navigation, so it may have been retired. I could not confirm this.

**Licensing:** As a U.S. government work, it is generally public domain. I did not find an explicit license statement.

## 6. Who uses it

- **Congress:** writing and changing farm bills. NASS says many national and state programs are designed or allocated using census data, including soil conservation projects, cooperative extension funding and research funding.
- **USDA agencies:** the Economic Research Service, Agricultural Research Service, Farm Service Agency, Risk Management Agency, Natural Resources Conservation Service, Rural Development, Foreign Agricultural Service and World Agricultural Outlook Board. The Bureau of Economic Analysis also uses it and submitted a comment on the 2027 collection.
- **NASS itself:** the census provides the list of farms used for all NASS surveys. Without the census, NASS says, its ongoing reports degrade.
- **State and local governments:** state agriculture departments, county planners, extension services and land-grant universities.
- **Private sector:** agribusiness, lenders, cooperatives, input suppliers and ag-tech firms (market sizing, siting, distribution).
- **Researchers:** economists, economic historians, environmental scientists (land use, nutrients, watersheds) and rural sociologists.
- **Advocates and media:** local-food, equity (for example, Black and Native farmers' land tenure), conservation and farmworker groups, plus journalists.
- **Genealogists, historians and lawyers:** mostly through the historical archive.

## 7. Methods and quality notes for data scientists

- **How it's collected:** a mail list is built from NACS and other sources. Responses come by mail, online (agcounts.usda.gov) and phone or in-person follow-up. Some areas are counted entirely in person.
- **Response rate trend:** 61% in 2022. My recollection, which I did not re-check, is roughly 72% in 2017 and 80% in 2012. Response to NASS's other surveys has fallen to about 30%.
- **Coverage adjustment (from memory, not re-checked this session):** since 1997, NASS has weighted results for undercoverage, nonresponse and misclassification. It uses an independent area-based survey and capture-recapture methods. In 2027 this is the Agricultural Coverage Evaluation Survey (ACES). Published numbers are therefore model-adjusted. Check each census's Appendix A methodology before analysis.
- **Suppression:** "(D)" cells are withheld to protect individual operations, and this is common in small counties. Coefficients of variation are published for many items. Look up the codes (D), (Z), (NA) and (X) before computing totals.
- **Comparability breaks:**
  - The 2017 producer definitions.
  - The 2027 race and ethnicity question now follows OMB's 2024 standard: one combined question that adds a Middle Eastern or North African category. This will break the 2027 race series.
  - The non-inflation-adjusted $1,000 threshold means more tiny operations count as farms over time.
  - Geographic boundaries (counties, districts) change between censuses.
- **Timing:** data for reference year X is collected in early X+1 and released around 14 months later.

## 8. Preservation and archiving

- **NASS Historical Archive** (nass.usda.gov/AgCensus/archive; originally agcensus.mannlib.cornell.edu): digitized reports for 1840–2002. NASS warns that some publications are missing because of incomplete record keeping.
- **ICPSR 35206:** "United States Agriculture Data, 1840–2012" by Haines, Fishback and Rhode, doi:10.3886/ICPSR35206.v4. County-level, machine-readable, with codebooks.
- **IPUMS NHGIS:** county data for 1840–1950, with matching boundary files.
- **Library of Congress and Federal Depository Libraries:** print volumes.
- **Original farm-level schedules (from memory):** 1850–1880 agricultural schedules survive at the National Archives and in state archives. Most 1890 schedules were lost after a 1921 fire, and the 1900–1920 agricultural schedules were destroyed. Modern farm-level records are confidential.
- **Suggested capture targets:**
  - Quick Stats bulk files
  - All 1997–2022 report PDFs and tables
  - Methodology appendices and questionnaires
  - The OMB filing documents for 0535-0226 (supporting statements, public comments)
  - Interactive maps, which are fragile web tools
- **Fragility signals:** tools quietly removed from site navigation, plus heavy staff losses.

## 9. Current risks and policy context (as of October 2026)

- **Staffing:** NASS shrank from 839 staff-years (FY2023) to a budgeted 389 (FY2026). Census-program staff fell from 230 to 100, with about $46 million in funding. The FY2027 request adds $2.5 million for the 2027 mail list (NACS sent to about 1 million operations) and the coverage survey (ACES).
- **Reorganization:** some Washington staff are moving to St. Louis and other regional hubs.
- **Earlier program cuts:**
  - In April 2024, budget limits led NASS to cut the July Cattle report and county estimates. Both were reinstated in March 2025.
  - In August 2025, NASS discontinued the Mink Survey and the Agricultural Labor Survey. Farm-wage data now come from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
- **Modernization push:**
  - February 2026: a public request for information on USDA statistical data products.
  - Summer 2026: a NASS review led by Kip Tom.
  - "Data Modernization Plan to Put Farmers First," announced at the Farm Progress Show (Sept. 1–3, 2026): more administrative data, satellite imagery, pre-filled forms and AI. It has no timeline.
  - None of this changes the legal requirement for the census, but it may shape how the 2027 census is run.
- **Warnings from statisticians:** the American Statistical Association says funding is insufficient for the 2027 census, citing record-low survey response and reduced quality.
- **Ongoing debates:** raising or inflation-indexing the farm threshold; undercounting of small, urban and minority-operated farms; how much suppression erodes county detail; respondent burden; and new questions. The 2027 filing includes a pilot on sexual orientation, gender identity and disability.
- **Ways to participate:**
  - NASS data users' meetings, including a virtual one announced October 1, 2026.
  - Federal Register comment periods.
  - Content requests for future censuses at nass.usda.gov/go/aginput.
  - Farmers can make sure they're counted at agcounts.usda.gov/getcounted.

## 10. Benefits to the public

- **Fair allocation:** it supports transparent, evidence-based farm policy and distribution of funds down to the county level.
- **Accountability:** it is a neutral record for the public, Congress and advocates to judge how farm policy affects different regions and groups.
- **Market fairness:** it gives small producers the same baseline information large firms have.
- **Research:** it is a 180-plus-year record of land use, rural economies and demographics.
- **Foundation for other statistics:** it anchors the accuracy of USDA's other statistics, which move markets.
- **Recognition:** it makes small, urban and underserved producers visible.

**Gaps in this report:** I hit my search limit before re-checking the methodology details, the 2012/2017 response rates and the fate of the original schedules, so those come from memory and are marked as such above. I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

# Risk Assessment: Census of Agriculture (USDA NASS)

The Census of Agriculture has strong legal protection, and its archive looks intact. The real risk is how well the agency can carry out the 2027 census. NASS has lost roughly 40–54% of its staff, survey response rates are at record lows, and several modernization and reorganization efforts are under way at once. This assessment reflects sources available through early October 2026.

**A correction to my earlier report:** I said the 2027 filing includes a pilot study on sexual orientation, gender identity (SOGI) and disability. That was wrong. The approved package lists that pilot as **"Removed."** The filing describes this as "removal of 2022 Census of Agriculture pilot study work."

**A note on the staffing tracker:** I couldn't get agency-level numbers from usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com. Its data loads through scripts the fetch tool couldn't run, and the site says it stopped updating on December 31, 2025. I used Office of Personnel Management (OPM), American Statistical Association (ASA) and USDA budget figures instead.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- The historical archive at nass.usda.gov/AgCensus/archive still holds reports from 1840 to 2002. The site's dropdown lists every census year from 1840 to 2022.
- The 2022 Race, Ethnicity and Gender Profiles are still online, last modified June 28, 2024. Other USDA demographic material was removed in 2025: the Equity Commission report disappeared, and the REGStats tool was taken down and then came back partly redacted (Farm Aid, Feb. 2025). REGStats is a USDA-wide tool that also shows Census of Agriculture figures, but I found no change to the census data itself.
- Copies exist outside NASS: ICPSR study 35206, IPUMS NHGIS, Cornell's Mann Library and Federal Depository Libraries.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- The link to the Census Data Query Tool is commented out of NASS's site menu. The underlying data is still available through Quick Stats and the PDF reports. I did not confirm whether the tool itself has been retired.

**Rating: No Known Issue.** I found no removed files or changed data. The missing query-tool link affects access, not the data.

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- The 2022 census was released on schedule on February 13, 2024. The follow-on studies were also on time or early. For example, the 2023 Irrigation report came out early (NASS notice, Sept. 25, 2024).
- OMB approved the 2027 collection (control number 0535-0226) "with change" on September 16, 2026. The approval runs through September 30, 2029.
- The draft 2027 form sets a due date of February 21, 2028. The mail-list surveys ran in 2024 and 2026, and the FY2027 budget funds a version sent to about 1 million operations, plus the coverage evaluation survey.

**Evidence for High Risk (on a strict reading):**
- The previous OMB approval expired September 30, 2024, and was not reinstated until September 2026, a gap of about two years. This is the normal pattern between census cycles: the 2022 census was also approved as a "reinstatement" in 2021. No census collection was due during the gap.

**Rating: No Known Issue.** I don't count the lapse because no collection was scheduled during it. A strictly literal reading of the rubric would make this High Risk.

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- The 2022 response rate was 61%. Response to other NASS surveys has fallen to about 30%. The March 2026 Prospective Plantings report hit a record-low 37.6% response.
- Corn-acreage revisions in January 2026 hurt confidence in NASS numbers (ASA comment on the USDA request for information; Reuters).
- The ASA warns that resources "are simply no longer sufficient."
- Census-program staff fell from 230 to 100 full-time equivalents (FY2027 USDA budget explanatory notes).
- Losing staff to relocation threatens how quickly the census can be processed.

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- NASS cut other programs: county estimates and the July Cattle report in 2024 (both later reinstated), and the Agricultural Labor Survey in August 2025.
- None of these cuts touched the census's own detail, timeliness or frequency.

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- The ASA says there has been "remarkably little impact on [NASS's] release schedule."
- The 2027 content keeps the full county-level detail and moves race and ethnicity to OMB's updated 2024 standard.

**Rating: Moderate Risk.** The risk is emerging and credible, but no reduction has happened yet.

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- The Census of Agriculture Act of 1997 (7 U.S.C. 2204g) explicitly requires a census every five years, and response is mandatory.
- Appropriations language sets aside up to $48.5 million for the census and requires 30 days' notice to Congress before NASS drops any program.
- USDA calls it "the only source of consistent, comparable data at the county, state and national levels." It underpins programs at eight or more USDA agencies, and it supplies the list of farms used for all other NASS surveys.

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- The law leaves detailed content to the Secretary.
- The modernization plan's greater use of administrative and satellite data could be presented as a partial substitute. Even so, no alternative source covers every farm and commodity at the county level.

**Rating: No Known Issue.**

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- NASS staffing fell from 839 full-time equivalents in FY2023 to 389 in FY2026, a 54% drop (ASA; FY2027 budget explanatory notes). OPM data show a drop of about 39.5% (806 to 484).
- More than 300 employees have left since January 2025 (Agri-Pulse).
- Census-program staff fell 57% (230 to 100).
- Positions are being moved to St. Louis and regional hubs. Staff had until July 8, 2026 to accept reassignment, with buyouts offered, and the ASA expects further losses (Federal News Network, June 2026; ASA midyear 2026 update).
- Many leadership posts are filled on an acting basis. In November 2025, four of seven NASS divisions had acting directors.

**Evidence for lower risk:**
- The budget is roughly flat: $187.85 million in FY2024, $185 million in FY2026, and $187.46 million requested for FY2027. Census funding went from $46.85 million to $46 million, with $48.5 million requested (+5.4%).
- Administrator Joseph Parsons has been in place since June 2024.

**Rating: High Risk.** Staff losses are well above the 40% threshold.

## 6. Policy

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- **February 2026:** Secretary Rollins issued a request for information on USDA data products.
- **Summer 2026:** a NASS review led by Kip Tom.
- **September 1, 2026:** the "Data Modernization Plan to Put Farmers First" announced more administrative data, pre-filled forms, AI, and satellite pilots. Officials said pilots would start this year, with transitions in 2027 and permanent changes the year after (Agweek, USDA press release).
- **April 2026:** USDA announced the reorganization of its Research, Education and Economics mission area, which includes NASS.
- The plan mostly targets crop estimates, not the census, but it overlaps in time with 2027 census operations.

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- The SOGI and disability pilot was dropped from the 2027 package. This is consistent with Administration priorities on gender, but the stated reason is that the 2022-era pilot work ended. The pilot was a research study, not published census data.
- Broader USDA moves on race and sex: the July 2025 rule ending race- and sex-based criteria in farm programs, and the REGStats redactions.

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- The core 2027 content, including sex, race and ethnicity, was kept.
- I found no negative policy note on the website and no executive-order-driven change to the collection.

**Rating: Moderate Risk.** Changes are planned and pending, but none so far has cut census content or publication.

Historical Data Availability: No Known Issue
Future Data Availability: No Known Issue
Data Quality: Moderate Risk
Statutory Context: No Known Issue
Staffing and Funding: High Risk
Policy: Moderate Risk
